title: Ro Khanna Wants a 'Second New Deal' — and He Pitched It to a Room Full of Graduates
excerpt: The Silicon Valley congressman used a Suffolk University commencement to lay out a sweeping economic vision: wealth taxes, Medicare for All, AI oversight, and what he calls economic patriotism.
body:
When Ro Khanna stepped to the podium at Suffolk University's commencement last week, few in the audience expected a campaign-style manifesto. What they got was a sweeping economic vision the California congressman called a "Second New Deal"—a programme that, if it ever reaches legislative text, would touch nearly every corner of American life, from billionaires' balance sheets to the algorithms powering Silicon Valley.

Khanna, an Indian-American Democrat who represents a crescent of Silicon Valley stretching from Cupertino to Fremont, laid out four pillars: a federal wealth tax on ultra-high-net-worth individuals, universal healthcare through Medicare for All, comprehensive regulation of artificial intelligence, and what he termed "economic patriotism"—a blend of industrial policy and antitrust enforcement designed to break what he described as the "political capture" of American democracy by corporate interests.

**The wealth tax**

Khanna's proposal goes further than previous Democratic tax plans. Rather than simply raising marginal income-tax rates, he called for a direct tax on accumulated wealth above a threshold he suggested could sit at $100 million. "The New Deal taxed income. A Second New Deal must tax wealth," he told the graduating class. "Income taxes alone cannot address a system in which the richest Americans hold more wealth than the bottom half of the country combined."

The idea is not new—Senators Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders have floated similar proposals—but Khanna's framing links it explicitly to AI-era inequality, arguing that machine-learning-driven productivity gains will further concentrate wealth unless the tax code catches up.

**AI regulation and Silicon Valley's unease**

For a congressman whose district includes the headquarters of Apple and several major AI labs, the call for regulation is politically fraught. Khanna proposed a federal AI oversight body with the power to mandate algorithmic audits, enforce transparency in training data, and set liability standards for AI-caused harms. He also called for a moratorium on "autonomous weapons-grade AI" and urged the federal government to invest $50 billion in public AI research, ensuring that the technology's benefits are not monopolised by a handful of corporations.

The speech places Khanna at an interesting crossroads within the Democratic Party. He has long cultivated ties to the tech industry—his campaign donors include prominent Valley executives—yet his regulatory stance puts him closer to the party's progressive wing than to its techno-optimist centre.

**Medicare for All**

The healthcare plank is perhaps the most familiar. Khanna reiterated his support for a single-payer system that would replace private insurance with a government-run programme, arguing that the United States spends more per capita on healthcare than any other developed nation while delivering worse outcomes.

For the Indian-American diaspora, the proposal has particular resonance. Many NRI professionals work in industries where employer-sponsored health insurance is a golden handcuff, tying workers to jobs they might otherwise leave. A universal system, Khanna argued, would "unleash entrepreneurship" among immigrant communities that already punch above their weight in starting businesses.

**A diaspora constituency**

Khanna's speech was also, unmistakably, an early sounding of a possible 2028 presidential campaign. He is one of the most prominent Indian-American voices in Congress, and his policy platform is calibrated to appeal both to progressive activists and to the aspirational middle class that forms the backbone of the Indian-American electorate. His framing of economic patriotism—supporting American manufacturing, investing in education, and curbing the influence of monopolies—echoes concerns voiced by diaspora voters who worry about job security in an era of AI disruption and offshoring.

Whether a Second New Deal has any chance of passing the current Congress is another matter. Republicans control the House, and even some Democrats blanch at the price tag of universal healthcare. But as a statement of ambition—and as a signal of where the party's Indian-American standard-bearer wants to take the conversation—Khanna's Suffolk address was hard to ignore.
